title: Cap. IX Arg. 1 Resp.: Bannes and Lombard — praeterition manifests liberty in dispensing supernatural goods
pass_a_gloss: Rightly Bannes, This passing by or reprobation of certain persons, others being elected, is manifestative of the greatest liberty which the Divine will has concerning the dispensation of supernatural goods, On 1, question 23, article 5, page 293. But now it is by no means alien from Divine wisdom, as also its other attributes, so also to manifest this attribute of liberty in dispensing the highest good unto men. Whence Lombard, book 1, distinction 41, God reprobated whom he willed, not on account of future merits which he foresaw, yet by a most right truth, removed from our senses. These things concerning the Major.
pass_b_english: Bannes puts it well: this praeterition or reprobation of some persons, others being elect, manifests the greatest liberty the divine will has in dispensing supernatural goods (on ST I, q. 23 a. 5, p. 293). Nor is it alien to divine wisdom — as with his other attributes — to manifest this attribute of liberty in dispensing the highest good to men. So Lombard (Sentences 1, dist. 41): God reprobated whom he willed, not for future merits he foresaw — yet by a most right truth, remote from our senses. So much for the Major.
source_text: Recte Bannes, Haec praeteritio sive reprobatio aliquarum personarum, aliis electis, est manifestativa maximae libertatis quam habet Divina voluntas circa dispensationem bonorum supernaturalium, In 1. quaest. 23. art. 5. pag. 293. Jam vero haud alienum est a sapientia Divina, sicuti et reliqua sua attributa, ita et hoc libertatis attributum in summo bono dispensando hominibus manifestare. Unde Lombardus, lib. 1. dist. 41, Reprobavit Deus quos voluit, non propter futura merita quae praevideret, veritate tamen rectissima, a nostris sensibus remota. Haec de Majore.
